claims.text: The target alloy is a solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.

In high-entropy alloys outside canonical Nb-Ta and known titanium-rich systems, superconducting transition temperature is predominantly governed by local lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Local lattice distortions modulate electron-phonon coupling strength.
Increasing local strain while avoiding phase separation enhances the electron-phonon coupling constant.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling caused by increased local strain raises Tc relative to the baseline alloy.
The starting material is a single-phase high-entropy solid solution.
A titanium-rich alloy based on heavy transition metals is offered as an example starting material.
Substituting one constituent with a chemically similar element of slightly different atomic radius will increase atomic-size mismatch and local lattice strain while preserving the solid solution.
Enhanced local lattice distortion can be detected through broadened XRD peaks and increased local-strain contrast in high-resolution TEM.
Added lattice distortions locally modify the alloy's vibrational modes.
The modified vibrational modes increase electron-phonon coupling.
Up to an optimal distortion level, stronger electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper pairing and elevates Tc.
Excessive distortion may produce electronic scattering or localization that adversely affects the density of states at the Fermi level.
The strain-enhanced alloy will have a higher Tc than the baseline alloy.
The Tc shift may be on the order of tens of kelvins.
The proposed effect applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and phase separation, precipitation, and localization do not dominate.
Failure of reproducibly increased lattice distortion to produce a significant Tc increase, including no change or a decrease, would reject the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis defines its target as outside known titanium-rich systems, but the example starting material is explicitly a titanium-rich alloy based on heavy transition metals.

The hypothesis calls the baseline 'undeformed,' whereas the initial-state and baseline descriptions acknowledge inherent atomic-size variation, native chemical disorder, and native lattice distortion. This makes 'undeformed' inconsistent unless it is intended only to mean 'without deliberate added distortion.'
